corrections.reason: Qualify evidence and state assumptions behind v=E/B.

marks: The sharp shadow supports straight-line travel in a field-free region. Paddle-wheel motion is supporting evidence of energy/momentum transfer; by itself it is not a unique quantitative demonstration of electron mass.
Deflection towards the positive plate, reversing with polarity, shows the particles are negatively charged.
Balanced forces: eE = evB, so v = E ÷ B = 3.0 × 10⁴ ÷ 1.5 × 10⁻³ = 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
With the magnetic field alone, evB = mv²/r, so e/m = v ÷ (Br) = 2.0 × 10⁷ ÷ (1.5 × 10⁻³ × 0.0758) = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.
The same behaviour for different gases and metals suggests a universal particle (the electron); e/m is only a ratio, so charge and mass separately need another measurement.
patch.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results from a demonstration with a cathode-ray tube. For the speed measurement the electric and magnetic deflections cancel when E = 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 1.5 × 10⁻³ T. With the magnetic field alone, the beam moves on a circle of radius 0.0758 m. Assume mutually perpendicular electric/magnetic fields with the beam perpendicular to both; use the nonrelativistic model.

corrections.reason: Make gas-pressure and Ar versus molar-mass assumptions explicit.

marks: Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂, so n(Mg) = n(H₂).
The gas is saturated with water vapour: p(H₂) = 101.3 − 3.2 = 98.1 kPa.
M(Mg) = 0.0480 g / n(Mg) = about24.44 g mol-1; the corresponding dimensionless relative atomic mass is Ar≈24.4 (using the g mol-1 numerical equivalence).
Ignoring vapour pressure overestimates the hydrogen and gives Ar = 23.7 (too low); an oxide layer means less magnesium metal reacts per measured gram, so the hydrogen is lower and Ar is too high.
patch.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional completed results: 0.0480 g of magnesium reacted completely with excess dilute acid and 49.6 cm³ of hydrogen was collected over water at 298 K. The atmospheric pressure was 101.3 kPa and the vapour pressure of water at 298 K is taken as 3.2 kPa. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume collected-gas pressure equals atmospheric pressure before the water-vapour subtraction (liquid levels equal or hydrostatic correction already applied).

corrections.reason: Parenthesise the full wavelength denominator; no final numerical change.

marks: A contains potassium (lilac); a trace of sodium can hide this colour.
B contains sodium (golden-yellow, near 589 nm).
C contains calcium (brick-red) and E contains barium (apple-green).
D (crimson) is shown by both lithium and strontium, so the colour cannot decide between them without another test.
Excited electrons return to lower levels and emit light: E=hc/λ=(6.63×10^-34 ×3.00×10^8)/(589×10^-9)=3.38×10^-19 J per photon; multiplying by6.02×10^23/1000 gives about203 kJ mol-1.

corrections.reason: Repair the unsupported unique identification without inventing extra observations.

marks: X is consistent with carbonate, but the supplied colourless-gas/limewater/no-acidified-barium-precipitate pattern also fits sulfite; a selective additional record is required.
Y contains sulfate: it gives a white barium sulfate precipitate that is insoluble in acid.
Z contains thiosulfate: acid gives a pungent gas (sulfur dioxide) and a fine pale yellow-white precipitate of sulfur.
Both CO2 and SO2 can make limewater cloudy. Gas odour is not an appropriate student identification method; use an additional supplied chemical distinction such as the SO2 reducing response.
Prior acidification removes carbonate/sulfite interferences because their barium precipitates dissolve/react in dilute acid, whereas sulfate gives acid-resistant BaSO4.
patch.question: Identify Y and Z. Explain why X is consistent with carbonate but not uniquely established, why limewater alone is inconclusive, and why acidification helps the sulfate comparison.

corrections.reason: Qualify the scope of the negative control.

marks: In air magnesium forms white magnesium oxide and a yellow-grey magnesium nitride.
Equations: 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂ and Mg₃N₂ + 6H₂O → 3Mg(OH)₂ + 2NH₃.
Damp red litmus turning blue shows an alkaline gas (ammonia), so nitrogen from the air was combined in the ash.

Provided the Mg source, water and handling are matched and the only intended difference is atmosphere, the negative pure-oxygen control supports nitrogen from air as the explanation; it does not categorically exclude every possible contamination or procedural difference.
The results show that nitrogen is present, not how much; litmus detects an alkaline gas, so a second test such as white fumes with hydrochloric acid supports ammonia.
patch.transfer_answer: Under matched materials and handling, the negative oxygen control supports air nitrogen as the source of ammonia. It is supporting evidence rather than an absolute exclusion of all contamination.

corrections.reason: Limit acidification claim to acid-reactive interferences; halide assignments and AgF transfer are correct.

marks: X is chloride: white silver chloride, soluble in dilute ammonia.
Y is bromide: cream silver bromide, soluble only in concentrated ammonia.
Z is iodide: yellow silver iodide, insoluble in both.
Nitric acid removes acid-reactive interferences such as carbonate, while nitrate does not itself precipitate Ag+. This does not mean every possible interfering ion is removed.
Colours are subjective and shade into each other, so solubility in ammonia is a second line of evidence; silver fluoride is soluble, so fluoride gives no precipitate.

patch.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results for three isomeric C₄ alcohols oxidised by warm acidified potassium dichromate(VI). No student handling is involved. The product-identification record for alcohol1 refers to its independently identified initial aldehyde oxidation product, before further oxidation.
marks: Alcohol 1 is primary: it is oxidised to an aldehyde, which gives the silver mirror.
Alcohol 2 is secondary: it is oxidised to a ketone, which reacts with 2,4-DNPH but not with Tollens' reagent.
Alcohol 3 is tertiary: the carbon bearing the –OH has no hydrogen, so it resists oxidation.
The orange dichromate(VI) is reduced to green chromium(III) when an alcohol is oxidised.

Green dichromate-reduction colour alone cannot distinguish primary from secondary alcohols. Hydrogen bonding raises alcohol boiling points; the ethanol78degC/propane-42degC comparison is associated background, not an extra measurement from these C4 records.
patch.transfer_answer: Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation by acidified dichromate under the ordinary conditions assumed here.

marks: Phenol forms phenoxide with OH-. No CO2 effervescence from carbonate means it does not drive the full carbonate-to-carbonic-acid/CO2 process under this comparison. This does not exclude some carbonate-to-hydrogencarbonate proton transfer.
Bromine water is decolourised at once with a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, because the –OH group activates the ring.
The phenoxide charge is delocalised into the ring, stabilising the ion, which makes phenol more acidic than ethanol.

Violet colour with neutral FeCl3 supports phenolic chemistry but is not absolutely unique. The weak-acid calculation assumes[H+]≈sqrt(Ka c), negligible water autoionisation and small dissociation relative to c.

patch.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional test records for three liquids A, B and C. No student handling is involved. Assume successful validated tests, no interfering compounds, and restrict candidates to simple aldehydes, ketones and monohydric alcohols. Interpret negatives only within that defined candidate set.

marks: Percentage ionisation = 1.32 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.100 × 100 = 1.3%.
Let c0=0.100mol dm-3 and x=[H+]=10^-2.88. Then Ka=x^2/(c0-x)≈1.76×10^-5mol dm-3 in the concentration approximation.
The hydrochloric acid [H⁺] is 0.100, about 76 times larger, so ethanoic acid is a weak acid that ionises only partly.

CO2 evolution from carbonate is consistent with the stated carboxylic-acid behaviour. It does not by itself measure Ka. pH-meter calibration, temperature, activities and contamination limit the inferred Ka.

corrections.reason: Qualify stability statement to the supplied aqueous practical context.

marks: In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton.
The factor is 10^(10.7 − 4.6) = 10^6.1 = 1.3 × 10⁶ (the ethylammonium ion is that many times weaker as an acid, so ethylamine is the far stronger base).
Bromine water gives an immediate white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline because the –NH₂ group activates the ring.

Cold aqueous conditions help preserve the aromatic diazonium intermediate; warming accelerates decomposition with N2 evolution and can reduce the subsequent dye signal. This is not a universal stability boundary for every diazonium salt.
The orange-red azo dye shows coupling, but these are group tests; a single observation does not identify a compound.
patch.transfer_answer: Cold aqueous conditions slow decomposition of the diazonium intermediate; warming can accelerate N2 loss and reduce the subsequent coupling signal.

corrections.reason: Use measuredE instead of unjustifiedE°; display unrounded conversions and precise reference cancellation.

marks: E (versus SHE) = E (versus SCE) + 0.241 V.
E(Cu versusSHE)=+0.100+0.241=+0.341V, about+0.34V at the original reading precision.
E(Zn versusSHE)=-1.000+0.241=-0.759V, about-0.76V at the original reading precision.
Ecell=+0.341-(-0.759)=+1.100V, equal to the original reference-scale difference+0.100-(-1.000)=+1.100V. The reference cancels.

These are potentials at the stated conditions.1.00mol dm-3 does not guarantee unit ion activity, so label themE rather thanE° unless standard activities are established. SCE potential depends on filling composition and temperature.
patch.question: Convert both measured potentials to the SHE scale, calculate Ecell for the Cu–Zn cell at the stated conditions, show reference cancellation, and explain why1.00mol dm-3 does not alone establish standard activities.
patch.transfer_answer: E=-0.200+0.241=+0.041V, approximately+0.04V at the original reading precision.

corrections.reason: Correct saltingout explanation and remove misleading premature-rounding substitution.

marks: Triglyceride + 3KOH → glycerol + 3 potassium soap (carboxylate salt).
Saponification value = 6.70 × 10⁻³ × 56.1 × 1000 mg ÷ 2.00 g = 188 mg g⁻¹.
n(fat)=0.00670/3=0.00223333mol; retain this unrounded value. M(fat)=2.00/0.00223333=895.5g mol-1, or896g mol-1 to3significant figures.

Concentrated NaCl can salt out soap by reducing its solubility in the concentrated electrolyte, separating a soap-rich fraction from glycerol/excess alkali. For the potassium soap in this problem, NaCl is not simply a common-K+ ion effect. Free fatty acids would alter the stoichiometric inference.

corrections.reason: Replace guaranteed thermal protection and one-direction yield claim with defensible limits.

marks: For immiscible liquids the total vapour pressure is the sum, p(total) = p(oil) + p(water); the mixture boils when this equals atmospheric pressure.
In the vapour, n(oil) ÷ n(water) = 7.0 ÷ 94.3 = 0.0742.
Mass ratio = 0.0742 × 136 ÷ 18.0 = 0.561 g of oil per gram of water in the distillate.

The stated immiscible-component model permits co-distillation below the individual normal boiling temperatures. This can reduce thermal degradation risk; it does not guarantee zero decomposition. Incomplete equilibration/collection and nonideal behaviour can change actual recovery.

corrections.reason: Clarify chemically distinct effects of water and free fatty acids.

marks: Triglyceride + 3CH₃OH → 3 methyl esters + glycerol (ratio 1 : 3 : 3 : 1).
Theoretical ester = 3 × 0.11294 × 296.5 = 100.46 g.

Free fatty acids consume base to form soap; water can promote hydrolysis and soap formation. Incomplete equilibrium conversion and product losses can also lower isolated ester yield. Excess methanol favours ester formation in the ideal equilibrium model.
